tldr: By combining a VLA policy that simultaneously predicts both geometric motion goals and contact-force commands with an RL-based whole-body controller boosted by trajectory optimization (TO) torques, this framework achieves flexible and precise language-conditioned force regulation in humanoid whole-body control.
hero_caption: The overall Opt2VLA pipeline. Trajectory optimization (TO) generates physically consistent torque and force trajectories, which serve as supervision to train a force-conditioned RL whole-body controller (FCT). Data collected from executing this controller in simulation is then used to fine-tune a VLA policy, enabling a real humanoid to simultaneously predict end-effector positions and contact forces from language instructions.
overview:
To be useful in daily environments, humanoids must handle contact-rich tasks like wiping tables, pushing boxes into shelves, and lifting boxes of varying weights. However, conventional Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models output only geometric motion goals—such as end-effector positions or joint angles—without explicitly considering interaction forces. As a result, they cannot modulate force based on language instructions (e.g., wiping gently vs. scrubbing firmly), and external forces during contact often destabilize low-level motion controllers.

To address this, the authors propose Opt2VLA, a framework that introduces explicit target contact forces directly into the VLA action interface. A high-level multi-task VLA policy jointly predicts geometric goals and contact-force references from vision, language, and torque history. At the low level, a reinforcement learning (RL) whole-body controller, trained using dynamically grounded torque supervision from trajectory optimization (TO), tracks both the position and force commands simultaneously.

Evaluated in simulation and on a physical Digit humanoid across three contact-rich tasks (table wiping, shelf box pushing, and lifting boxes of different weights), Opt2VLA significantly improved force regulation accuracy and stability over motion-only baselines, successfully modulating interaction forces according to language prompts like "gently", "firmly", and "strongly".
contributions: Proposed a novel humanoid control formulation introducing explicit continuous contact-force goals alongside geometric motion targets at the VLA-to-whole-body controller interface.
Developed a force-conditioned RL whole-body controller (FCT) that achieves high force tracking accuracy using physically consistent joint torque supervision from trajectory optimization (TO).

Built an automated data collection pipeline that leverages TO and trained controller rollouts—without teleoperation—to produce a large-scale multimodal dataset with aligned vision, language, and force targets.
Demonstrated closed-loop language-conditioned force modulation and contact-rich Sim-to-Real transfer on physical Digit humanoid hardware.

sections.heading: Why Do Humanoids Need to Understand Force Commands?
sections.summary: Operating alongside humans requires precise force control, not just position accuracy. This section outlines the limitations of existing motion-only VLAs and introduces Opt2VLA, a hierarchical framework featuring explicit force commands.
sections.details:
When humanoid robots perform autonomous tasks in human environments—such as pushing objects into shelves, wiping surfaces, or grasping heavy loads—delivering sustained, appropriate contact forces is vital for stability and safety.

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have accelerated progress in planning end-effector poses and joint trajectories from natural language instructions. However, most existing methods restrict their action representations to geometric motions, lacking an interface to explicitly command interaction forces. Even when motions are geometrically identical, required force levels vary widely depending on the task context and object properties. Moreover, visual observations often degrade after contact due to occlusion or camera shake, making purely vision-based feedback fragile.

To solve this, the paper introduces Opt2VLA, which outputs both geometric motion goals (where to move) and contact-force references (how hard to press) directly from the VLA. The low-level whole-body controller uses reinforcement learning (RL) guided by physically grounded joint torques from whole-body trajectory optimization (TO), ensuring accurate force regulation. By running this controller in simulation, the framework collects large-scale, force-labeled multimodal data to fine-tune the VLA without expensive human teleoperation.

sections.heading: Whole-Body Control Meets VLAs: Progress and Gaps
sections.summary: This section reviews classical whole-body control (model-based and RL) alongside recent humanoid VLA research, showing how Opt2VLA sets itself apart by explicitly planning target forces at the high level rather than relying on motion-only tracking or reactive feedback.
sections.details:
Related work spans two main areas: humanoid whole-body control (WBC) and vision-language-action (VLA) models for humanoids.

### Humanoid Whole-Body Control (WBC)
Traditional model-based control and optimization methods rely heavily on accurate dynamic models and contact sequence assumptions, making real-time deployment under real-world uncertainties difficult. In contrast, RL-based approaches frequently rely on motion retargeting from human demonstrations. This introduces dynamic inconsistencies due to the embodiment gap and provides no explicit force or torque supervision. While recent methods like Opt2Skill use trajectory optimization (TO) to generate dynamically feasible references for RL, they remain confined to tracking geometric motion goals without the ability to adjust contact forces at the task level.

### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) for Humanoids
Adapting large pretrained VLA models to humanoids (e.g., Open6DOR, GR00T) has gained significant momentum. Most of these models plan hand positions or joint trajectories, delegating physical interaction entirely to lower-level controllers. While some tabletop manipulation works feed joint torques or tactile signals as inputs, they merely observe current contact states rather than planning how much force should be exerted for the task. Opt2VLA fundamentally differs by inferring necessary contact forces directly from language and vision and sending them explicitly to the low-level controller.

sections.heading: The Opt2VLA Architecture: Grounding Language into Forces
sections.summary: A detailed look at how the VLA outputs both motion and force targets, how the RL-based force-conditioned controller (FCT) tracks them using TO torque supervision, and how trajectory optimization generates physically consistent training data.
sections.details:
Opt2VLA employs a hierarchical structure with a clear division between high-level VLA planning and low-level whole-body execution.

### III-A Explicit Force-Commanded VLA Policy
The VLA policy builds on the pretrained GR00T-N1.7 model. Taking language instructions $l$, visual images $I_t$, robot state history $\mathbf{s}_{t-K:t}$, and measured joint torque history $\bm{\tau}_{t-K:t}$ as inputs, it simultaneously predicts 3D end-effector position goals $\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{t:t+H}^{\mathrm{ee}}$ and contact normal force references $\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{t:t+H}$ across a prediction horizon $H$.
Torque inputs are processed via a dedicated torque encoder and added to the action tokens. An auxiliary training head predicting future measured joint torques is added to encourage the model to learn contact-relevant representations. Training data is collected automatically from simulation rollouts of the low-level controller, labeled with three language-conditioned force levels: "gently" (low), "firmly" (medium), and "strongly" (high).

### III-B Force-Conditioned Whole-Body Controller (FCT) with Torque Guidance
The low-level controller is trained as an RL policy (FCT) using an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup. Actor observations $o_t^{\mathrm{actor}}$ include end-effector targets $\mathbf{p}_t^{\mathrm{ee}}$, target contact forces $\mathbf{F}_t^{\mathrm{ref}}$ (augmented with Gaussian noise for robust Sim-to-Real transfer), robot proprioception, and joint torque history. The policy outputs default joint position offsets, converted to torques via an internal high-frequency PD control loop.
The reward function includes motion tracking $r_t^{\mathrm{motion}}$, target force tracking $r_t^{\mathrm{force}}$, regularization terms $r_t^{\mathrm{reg}}$, and a torque tracking reward $r_t^{\mathrm{torque}}$ referencing TO solutions. This torque reward is used purely as privileged information during Critic training and is not required during real-robot deployment.

### III-C Generating Supervision via Trajectory Optimization (TO)
Using contact-implicit Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) based on Pinocchio and Crocoddyl, the system computes whole-body motions and joint torques offline under floating-base dynamics, friction cones, and actuator limits. This produces dynamically consistent force and torque reference trajectories for controller training.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Precise Force Tracking and Seamless Language Modulation
sections.summary: Evaluated on a Digit humanoid across table wiping, shelf box pushing, and box lifting tasks. The TO-guided FCT controller achieved the best force tracking accuracy, and integrating the VLA successfully modulated contact forces based on language prompts in real hardware tests.
sections.details:
Opt2VLA was evaluated in both simulation and real-world experiments using a Digit humanoid (20 actuated degrees of freedom, ~48 kg).

### Low-Level Controller Force Performance
Three controllers were compared: (1) Motion-only tracking (MO), (2) Force-conditioned control (FC), and (3) Force-conditioned control with torque guidance (FCT, proposed).
- **Table Wiping**: MO exerted a roughly constant force with high variance despite varying target forces. FC separated force tiers but had noticeable errors. FCT achieved the lowest tracking error and smallest variance, maintaining stable contact.
- **Shelf Box Pushing**: When pushing a box flush against a shelf wall, FCT achieved the sharpest distribution with an average error of $4.2 \pm 5.5$ N.
- **Box Lifting**: For boxes weighing 0.5 kg, 1.0 kg, and 2.0 kg, FCT preserved an almost ideal linear relationship between commanded and exerted force, recording a grasping force error of $0.9 \pm 1.0$ N.

### Closed-Loop VLA Evaluation and Ablations
Nine VLA variants were benchmarked in simulation. Performance was measured by Joint Success Rate (Joint SR), requiring both task completion and force regulation within the designated prompt band (gentle: 0–9 N, firm: 5–16 N, strong: 12–22 N) with mean error under 5 N.
A motion-only input baseline (C0) reached only 40.0% Joint SR. In contrast, the proposed configuration (C7)—incorporating a dedicated torque encoder, observation history, and auxiliary future-torque prediction loss—reached an 82.2% Joint SR (90.0% task success rate). Simply concatenating torques into the state vector (C4: 27.8%) proved ineffective, highlighting the importance of the dedicated encoder.

### Physical Digit Hardware Validation
Across 30 real-world trials using external sensors, the FCT controller exhibited high linear correlation with commanded targets ($R^2=0.98$ for table wiping, $R^2=0.70$ for box pushing, and $R^2=0.80$ for box lifting). Furthermore, end-to-end VLA tests confirmed that the robot distinctly altered its exerted contact force when prompted with "gently", "firmly", or "strongly".

sections.heading: Conclusion: Unlocking Humanoid Autonomy through Coordinated Motion and Force
sections.summary: Opt2VLA demonstrates that combining an explicit force-motion interface with TO-supervised reinforcement learning sets a new benchmark for language-driven humanoid manipulation in contact-rich tasks.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Opt2VLA, a framework bridging language-vision planning and humanoid whole-body execution through explicit contact-force commands.

By generating dynamically feasible motions and torques via trajectory optimization (TO) in simulation, training a force-conditioned RL controller, and fine-tuning a VLA on its rollouts, the system achieves strong contact adaptability without relying on expensive human teleoperation data. Experiments quantitatively validated that the dedicated torque encoder and auxiliary future torque prediction enable force modulations impossible with pure motion tracking, transferring successfully Sim-to-Real to the Digit humanoid.

Future work aims to extend this framework to highly dynamic contact tasks and multi-point contact manipulation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Reward Formulations, Domain Randomization, and Evaluation Details
sections.summary: Provides comprehensive implementation details on RL reward components, simulation domain randomization ranges, real-robot external sensor setups, and formal evaluation criteria.
sections.details:
The appendix provides full implementation parameters for reproducibility.

### Reward Formulation and Domain Randomization for Sim-to-Real
The controller's reward includes tracking end-effector, joint, and base positions/velocities, along with target contact force tracking ($r^{\mathrm{force}}$) and TO reference torque tracking ($r^{\mathrm{torque}}$). For Sim-to-Real transfer, physical parameters such as link mass ($\pm 10\%$), center of mass, joint friction, damping, and actuator delays (0–40 ms) were randomized extensively. Gaussian noise was also added to target end-effector positions and force commands to build robustness against VLA prediction noise.

### Real-Robot Protocols and Contact Phase Detection
On physical hardware, ground-truth forces were captured using an external Bertec force plate (for table wiping) and a thin SensX 160 sensor. These sensor readings were reserved strictly for evaluation and never provided to the policy. Data processing used filtered signals to identify contact onset and detachment, while tracking metrics (MAE, $R^2$) were computed on baseline-corrected, unfiltered measurements.

takeaways: Explicitly predicting contact-force targets alongside geometric motions allows VLAs to modulate task-dependent forces even when motions appear identical.
Using joint torques from trajectory optimization (TO) as privileged training supervision for the RL controller (FCT) dramatically improves force tracking accuracy and contact stability.
Integrating force-torque feedback into VLAs requires a dedicated torque encoder and auxiliary future-torque prediction rather than simple vector concatenation.
A pipeline of "TO references → RL controller training → controller rollout collection" builds rich force-aware VLA datasets without expensive teleoperation.
limitations: Force commands are currently restricted to a 1D scalar normal force at a single contact point, rather than full spatial wrench control or multi-point grasping.
In real table wiping, lower-level tracking bias introduced a steady-state offset error in actual forces despite accurate VLA force targets.
Trajectory optimization still requires task-specific contact schedules and simplified models, presenting challenges for instantaneous generalization to arbitrary open-world setups.
